Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s confirmation of a new Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory has raised concerns among business owners over potential disruptions to activities, international travel, cross-border trade and investment, as authorities race to prevent the infection from spreading. Earlier on Tuesday, Ali Pate, the Minister of Health, confirmed one case of Ebola disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). According to the minister, the confirmed case involves a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda. He added that the patient is currently in isolation and receiving medical care at a private hospital in the FCT. However, the minister noted that contact tracing has commenced, with 44 close contacts identified so far, some of which include healthcare workers, patients, caregivers, and travel contacts. “The FG calls on all public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to be on high alert. Healthcare workers must maintain a high index of suspicion, promptly identify and isolate suspected cases, observe strict infection prevention and control measures, and immediately report suspected cases to public health authorities,” the minister noted. This has caused panic and tension for residents, especially business owners who fear for the financial implications the disease is capable of causing. The ongoing 2026 Ebola outbreak in Africa, driven by the Bundibugyo strain, has claimed at least 4,600 lives out of more than 9,500 recorded cases. Muda Yusuf, founder and chief executive officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), described the development as disturbing and warned that an uncontrolled outbreak could weaken investor confidence and damage Nigeria’s international business relationships. “If it is not contained, it will affect mobility, it will affect cross-border businesses, it will harm our relationship with international partners. It will affect investment, as people who want to come into the country would think twice before coming,” Yusuf told BusinessDay. He said prolonged uncertainty over the safety of travel and doing business in Nigeria could discourage foreign visitors and investors, with consequences for commercial activity and international partnerships. Jide Awe, a technology analyst, also warned that the outbreak could undermine business confidence and economic activity if it spreads beyond the initial case. 2014 Ebola crisis offers economic lessons The concerns revive memories of Nigeria’s 2014 Ebola outbreak, when fear of infection disrupted commercial activity even as health authorities worked to contain the virus. The World Bank estimated that the outbreak triggered declines in demand of between 20 and 40 per cent in some shopping centres and commercial businesses in Lagos. Nigeria’s experience during the 2014 Ebola outbreak illustrates how a public health emergency can affect businesses even when transmission is successfully contained. The World Bank’s report, The Economic Impact of the 2014 Ebola Epidemic: Short- and Medium-Term Estimates for West Africa, published on October 8, 2014, examined the effects of fear, reduced consumer demand, travel restrictions and higher operating costs on economic activity. Preliminary reports from shopping centres and commercial businesses in Lagos indicated that demand had fallen by between 20 and 40 per cent in some cases following the arrival of Ebola in Nigeria. The government spent approximately $13 million in direct response costs to contain the outbreak, according to the report. The World Bank credited effective coordination between federal and state authorities, alongside support from international partners, for Nigeria’s successful response. The outbreak resulted in 20 confirmed and probable cases and eight deaths. The World Health Organisation (WHO) declared Nigeria Ebola-free on October 20, 2014, after health authorities monitored 894 contacts without detecting further cases. The experience demonstrated the importance of rapid diagnosis, contact tracing, public communication and coordination between government agencies in limiting both the health and economic consequences of an outbreak. Congo faces more than $1bn economic shock The Democratic Republic of the Congo offers a warning of the potential economic consequences when an Ebola outbreak persists and disrupts commercial activity. A June 2026 assessment by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), titled Rapid Socioeconomic Assessment of Ebola Outbreak in the DRC, estimated that even if an outbreak were contained within the DRC and Uganda, the Congolese economy could suffer more than $1 billion in real gross domestic product losses, with about 55,000 jobs at risk. The assessment projected that 985,000 additional people could be pushed into poverty. Under a wider scenario involving regional spillovers and additional global shocks, economic disruption across the continent could cost up to $3.6 billion. Even under the more contained scenario, trade restrictions, transport delays, declining consumer confidence and interruptions to informal markets could reduce continental economic output by $2.37 billion. The poorest households would be particularly vulnerable because they have limited savings to cushion income losses. Women could also face disproportionate effects because they account for a substantial share of informal cross-border traders and frontline caregivers. The consequences could extend beyond commerce. The UNDP assessment warned that diverting resources from routine healthcare to the Ebola response could contribute to as many as 2,520 excess infant deaths in the DRC from causes unrelated to Ebola. These figures are projections under different scenarios, not final calculations of losses already incurred. They nevertheless illustrate how a public health emergency can affect employment, household incomes, trade and public finances. For Nigeria, the assessment reinforces the importance of containing infections early while avoiding unnecessary disruption to legitimate business activity. Containment critical to protecting the economy Beyond the immediate medical response, Nigeria’s ability to contain the case will be crucial to limiting potential disruption to commerce and international mobility. The World Bank’s 2014 analysis found that the economic damage from Ebola can extend beyond countries with confirmed cases as fear and uncertainty change consumer behaviour, disrupt transport and discourage travel. Yusuf warned that a prolonged outbreak could increase pressure on healthcare spending, interrupt business travel and discourage international visitors and investors. For an economy dependent on cross-border commercial relationships, such disruptions could affect business operations and investor sentiment if uncertainty persists beyond the period needed to contain the infection. Awe called for rapid contact tracing, timely laboratory testing, protection for healthcare workers and stronger infection prevention measures in hospitals and other healthcare facilities. He also stressed the importance of clear, consistent public communication to counter misinformation and prevent unnecessary panic. Coordination with airlines, border health authorities and neighbouring countries will be important in identifying potential exposures linked to international travel, Awe said. Any travel or border measures, he added, should be guided by public health evidence and designed to avoid unnecessary disruption to legitimate trade. Healthcare authorities must also ensure that emergency measures do not undermine routine medical services, including maternal and child healthcare, he said. Nigeria’s experience in 2014 showed that decisive containment could limit the duration of an emergency and help restore public confidence. The immediate priorities are to identify and monitor relevant contacts, prevent further transmission and communicate verified information to the public. One confirmed case does not establish a widespread outbreak. But for businesses and investors, the speed and effectiveness of the response will be central to determining whether the incident remains contained or develops into a wider source of economic uncertainty.
